# Obsidian Plugins That Most Effectively Recreate Notion’s Multi-View Databases

The closest single-plugin replacements for Notion’s Table, Board/Kanban, Calendar, and List database views are **Notion Bases** and **Note Database**. Both document all four views over the same Markdown notes and frontmatter, with inline editing, filters, sorting, grouping, formulas, relations, and rollups. Notion Bases has the broader Notion-like feature inventory, while Note Database is the stronger Obsidian-native alternative for editable Markdown-backed databases and migration from Obsidian Bases.

For a modular setup, **Power Bases plus Obsidian’s core Bases** is the strongest documented combination: core Bases supplies Table and List, while Power Bases adds Board/Kanban and Calendar. **Database Views for Obsidian** and the discontinued **Projects** plugin are close three-view alternatives, but neither documents List as part of its requested view set. **Dataview**, **Database Folder**, **Rowbase**, the classic **Kanban** plugin, and **Full Calendar Remastered** are valuable partial or specialized solutions, but they do not reproduce one shared Notion-style database by themselves.

No Obsidian option shown here provides complete Notion parity. The main gaps are collaboration and permissions, linked database preservation during migration, exact formula compatibility, consistent task-level records, and the polished integration of one database across every view.

This report first defines the Notion baseline, then maps the available Obsidian candidates against the four requested views. It explains how each stores data, whether views share the same records, and how editing propagates. It then compares filtering, grouping, formulas, relations, templates, mobile support, maintenance, performance, and migration before giving recommendations by use case. The comparison reflects the documented ecosystem status available for the September 13, 2026 snapshot.

## 1. What Notion’s multi-view database model actually requires

### Four views, one database

Notion databases are collections of pages. Each row, card, calendar item, or list entry is still the same underlying page, with properties attached to it and a body that can contain ordinary page content. Notion describes Table, Board, Calendar, List, Timeline, Gallery, and Chart as different ways to present database items rather than separate copies of the data. ([Notion’s database introduction](https://www.notion.com/help/intro-to-databases))

The four requested views have distinct purposes:

| Requested view | Notion’s behavior | What an Obsidian equivalent must reproduce |
|---|---|---|
| Table | Pages appear as rows and properties as columns. Cells can be edited directly. | A structured grid over records with editable properties. |
| Board/Kanban | Pages are grouped by a property such as status, assignee, priority, or type. Cards can move between groups. | A board whose cards represent the same records and whose movement writes to the grouping property. |
| Calendar | Pages are positioned by a date property. Dragging an item changes its date. | A date-driven view with write-back to the source record. |
| List | Pages appear in a compact list with selected properties. | A lightweight index over the same records, not a separate list file. |

Notion’s Board view is broader than a conventional task Kanban. It can group by status, assignee, priority, or other supported properties, and it supports filters, sorts, custom properties, sub-groups, card sizes, column ordering, and group calculations. ([Notion’s Board documentation](https://www.notion.com/help/boards))

Notion also gives each view its own property visibility, filters, sorts, grouping, layout, and page-opening behavior. A filter applied to a Board does not automatically become a filter on the Table or Calendar. ([Notion’s view, filter, and sort documentation](https://www.notion.com/help/views-filters-and-sorts))

That distinction matters when assessing Obsidian plugins. A plugin that merely renders a table, a separate Kanban file, and a calendar widget has not necessarily replicated Notion’s model. The stronger test is whether all four views are lenses over the same records, with changes made in one view visible in the others.

### Relations, rollups, and formulas are part of the baseline

Notion’s database usefulness extends beyond view labels. A relation property connects pages in one database to pages in another. Relations can be one-way or two-way, and edits made through a two-way relation appear in both databases. A rollup then aggregates a property from related pages. ([Notion’s relations and rollups documentation](https://www.notion.com/help/relations-and-rollups))

For example, a Projects database can relate to a Tasks database. The project can then roll up task estimates, count related tasks, or calculate the earliest and latest task dates. Notion supports calculations such as count, count values, unique values, percentages, sums, averages, medians, minimums, maximums, ranges, and date ranges, depending on the property type.

Even Notion has boundaries. Relation and formula properties cannot currently be used for Board grouping, and a rollup cannot roll up another rollup because of possible loops. Exporting relations to CSV produces plain-text URLs, and re-importing that CSV does not reconstruct the live relations. These limitations are useful comparison points: “Notion parity” does not mean that every platform must reproduce an unlimited relational engine, but it does mean that a candidate should expose a comparable way to connect and aggregate records.

### Notion begins with a bounded database; Obsidian usually begins with files

A key architectural difference is scope. Notion normally begins with an empty, explicitly created database to which pages are added. Obsidian Bases and many community plugins commonly begin with existing vault files and narrow them with folder, tag, property, or query filters. A forum comparison describes this as Notion adding entries from zero while Obsidian subtracts files from a broad starting set; the numbers are an analogy, not measured counts. ([Obsidian forum comparison](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/q-a-are-obsidian-bases-the-same-as-notion-database/112363))

That gives Obsidian more freedom: a database can combine notes from different folders or use an existing vault-wide metadata system. It also creates more schema responsibility. If one note uses `status`, another uses `Status`, and a third uses an inline Dataview field, a property-driven database may treat them as different fields or omit some records entirely.

For this comparison, an “effective” Notion replacement therefore needs to be judged on six questions:

1. Does it document all four requested presentations?
2. Do the views use the same notes, tasks, or rows?
3. Do edits write back to the same source records?
4. Can the user filter, sort, group, and calculate without rebuilding the data?
5. Does it support relationships, formulas, templates, and bulk operations?
6. Is it maintainable and practical on the user’s desktop, mobile devices, and vault size?

## 2. Coverage at a glance

### Candidate classifications

The ecosystem is not one homogeneous group. Some candidates are complete database engines, some are view extensions, and some are combinations of independent tools.

| Candidate | Status | Single plugin or combination | Overall fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Notion Bases** | Community plugin; active release material | Single plugin | Closest Notion-style feature breadth |
| **Note Database** | Community plugin; active 1.2.x release material | Single plugin | Closest Obsidian-native all-four alternative |
| **Core Bases** | Obsidian core plugin | Single core feature | Strong Table/List foundation, but incomplete four-view coverage |
| **Power Bases + Core Bases** | Community extension plus core plugin | Combined | Strongest documented modular four-view route |
| **Database Views for Obsidian** | Community project; release materials emphasize BRAT/manual installation | Single plugin | Strong Table/Board/Calendar near-match; List not documented |
| **Obsidian Projects** | Discontinued and removed from the Community Plugins list | Single plugin | Historically close, but not a current recommendation |
| **Dataview** | Community plugin | Single plugin | Excellent query-driven Table/List/Calendar; no Board |
| **Database Folder** | Community plugin; Dataview-dependent | Single plugin plus dependency | Strong editable Table and some Calendar/relational features |
| **Rowbase** | Community plugin | Single plugin | Standalone structured database with Table/Board/List; no standalone Calendar |
| **Dashboard Hub** | Community plugin | Combined workspace | All four visual surfaces, but not one shared database schema |
| **Kanban Action Planner + Core Bases** | Community extension plus core Bases | Combined | Strong Board/Calendar workflow over notes; broader coverage depends on core views |
| **Full Calendar Remastered + Tasks** | Two community plugins | Combined | Excellent task calendar; not a general four-view database |
| **Classic Kanban + Dataview/Calendar** | Multiple independent plugins | Combined | Flexible but synchronization is weak |
| **DataLoom** | Maintained fork claims continued development; original project discontinued | Single plugin | Database-oriented, but requested view coverage is not documented |

A checkmark in the next table means that the supplied documentation explicitly names the view. It does not mean that the view has full Notion-equivalent behavior.

| Candidate or solution | Table | Board/Kanban | Calendar | List |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Notion Bases | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Note Database | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Core Bases | ✓ | — | — | ✓ |
| Power Bases + Core Bases | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Database Views for Obsidian | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| Projects | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | — |
| Dataview | ✓ | — | ✓ | ✓ |
| Database Folder | ✓ | — | ✓ | ~ |
| Rowbase | ✓ | ✓ | — | ✓ |
| Dashboard Hub | ✓* | ✓* | ✓* | ✓* |
| Kanban Action Planner + Core Bases | ✓* | ✓ | ✓ | ✓* |
| Full Calendar + Tasks | — | — | ✓ | — |
| Classic Kanban | — | ✓ | — | — |

The asterisk means that the surface comes from a separate component or source model rather than a single database engine. Database Folder’s changelog mentions a Calendar view and a List editing API, but the available material does not establish that List API as a distinct List presentation. ([Database Folder changelog](https://rafaelgb.github.io/obsidian-db-folder/changelog/))

### The two all-four finalists

The most consequential result is that two plugins document the requested four-view set in one package:

- **Notion Bases**: Table, Board, Gallery, List, Calendar, Timeline, and Chart.
- **Note Database**: Table, Board, Gallery, List, Chart, Calendar, and Timeline.

Both say the views operate over the same Markdown notes and frontmatter. The decision between them is therefore less about basic coverage and more about feature emphasis, editing model, migration, dependencies, and confidence in the surrounding ecosystem.

## 3. The two closest single-plugin matches

### Notion Bases: the closest feature-breadth match

Notion Bases is a third-party Obsidian community plugin by bgarciamoura. It is not affiliated with Notion; the name describes its design goal. Its project documentation lists seven views: Table, Board (Kanban), Gallery, List, Calendar, Timeline/Gantt, and Chart. It also lists 18 column types, spreadsheet-style formulas, relations, lookups, rollups, subtasks, CSV import/export, and bulk row actions. ([Notion Bases project](https://github.com/bgarciamoura/obsidian-notion-bases-plugin))

#### Data model and shared records

Notion Bases turns a folder into a database. Each row is a Markdown file in that folder, and each column value is a frontmatter field in the note. The database schema and view configuration are stored in `_database.md`; configuration for embedded views is stored in the hosting note. ([Notion Bases data model](https://bgarciamoura.github.io/obsidian-notion-bases-plugin/))

This is an unusually close match to Notion’s “same pages, different views” model. A Table cell edit changes the note’s frontmatter. A Board drag changes a select or status value. A Calendar drag changes the date property. The same note then appears differently in the other views because the views reread the same file-backed properties.

The folder-based source is both a strength and a limitation. It gives the user a clear database boundary and keeps rows searchable as ordinary notes, but it makes the database more dependent on folder organization than Notion’s abstract database container. The supplied documentation does not establish a way to reproduce all of Notion’s linked data-source behavior or workspace-level permissions.

#### View behavior

The plugin’s view inventory maps cleanly to the requested alternatives:

- **Table** provides inline editing, resizable and reorderable columns, column pinning, multi-column sorting, aggregation, and bulk actions.
- **Board** groups by a select or status field and allows cards to move between columns.
- **Calendar** places notes on a monthly grid using a date field, creates notes with a prefilled date, and supports week-view event durations when an end-date field is configured.
- **List** provides one line per note with property chips.

The release material describes continuing work on practical details. Version 1.13.0 added conditional formatting for formula, lookup, and rollup columns; accepted several Notion-style formula names; added Calendar end dates; and ensured schema-less Board values were not silently dropped. ([Notion Bases release notes](https://github.com/bgarciamoura/obsidian-notion-bases-plugin/releases))

#### Database capabilities beyond the views

Notion Bases documents 18 column types, including title, text, number, select, multi-select, checkbox, date, URL, email, phone, status, formula, relation, lookup, rollup, image, audio, and video.

Its filtering system is type-aware and supports AND/OR groups. Sorting supports multiple columns with reorderable priority. A live aggregation footer can show Sum, Average, Min, Max, and Count. Bulk actions can delete, duplicate, or move selected rows. These are the kinds of details that make a view operational rather than merely decorative.

Relations link rows across databases, lookups pull a value from a related note, and rollups aggregate related values with seven documented functions: `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `count_values`, and `list`. Self-relations can represent hierarchical subtasks up to three levels. ([Notion Bases feature documentation](https://bgarciamoura.github.io/obsidian-notion-bases-plugin/))

The formula engine uses a spreadsheet-like syntax with functions such as `IF`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `CONCAT`, `LEFT`, and `ROUND`. The release notes also document support for names familiar to Notion users, including `dateBetween`, `dateSubtract`, `prop`, `length`, and `toNumber`. That improves migration familiarity, but similar function names do not prove identical semantics.

The plugin also supports live `{{column}}` placeholders in note bodies and optional auto-arrangement of rows into nested folders based on property values. Those features are useful for local workflows, although they are not direct equivalents of Notion buttons or automation rules.

#### Strengths

Notion Bases is strongest when the goal is a single, visually coherent, Notion-like database interface.

Its principal strengths are:

- All four requested views in one plugin.
- Additional Gallery, Timeline, and Chart views.
- A shared Markdown/frontmatter source of truth.
- Broad typed-property support.
- Relations, lookups, rollups, formulas, subtasks, summaries, and bulk actions.
- Independent filters, sorts, and visible fields per view.
- CSV import and export.
- No cloud database, telemetry, or proprietary row store.
- Desktop and mobile support, with an Obsidian 1.8.7 minimum documented by the project.
- Availability through the Community Plugins directory.
- A relatively familiar spreadsheet-style formula model for users coming from Notion, Excel, or Google Sheets.

#### Weaknesses and parity gaps

The plugin’s breadth should not be confused with exact Notion compatibility.

First, all rows remain Markdown files. That is excellent for ownership and portability, but it means that database structure depends on frontmatter consistency, file names, links, and folders. Renaming or moving records is a file operation, not an abstract database operation.

Second, the supplied material does not establish full collaboration, permissions, comments, database locking, or real-time multi-user editing. Obsidian Sync can synchronize vault files, but file synchronization is not equivalent to Notion’s shared workspace permissions.

Third, the documentation advertises formulas, relations, lookups, and rollups but does not provide a systematic compatibility test against Notion’s formula and rollup semantics. A Notion formula that uses unsupported functions may require rewriting even if the function names look similar.

Fourth, templates and automation are less fully documented than the view and column systems. Live placeholders and auto-arrange rules are useful, but they should not be treated as a complete replacement for Notion database buttons, automations, and workspace workflows.

Finally, no comparable independent large-vault performance result is supplied. The project claims local operation and mobile support, but the practical experience will still depend on the number of files, frontmatter complexity, images, relation resolution, and the speed of the user’s device.

### Note Database: the strongest Obsidian-native alternative

Note Database by pangy9 is another all-four single-plugin candidate. Its README lists seven views over the same notes: Table, Board, Gallery, List, Chart, Calendar, and Timeline. It describes the plugin as a local-first database-view system that keeps records, properties, and relations inside the user’s Markdown vault. ([Note Database README](https://github.com/pangy9/obsidian-note-database))

#### Data model and synchronization

A Note Database database can be stored as a normal Markdown file marked with `db_view: true`. The database file contains configuration, while records and their property values remain in ordinary Markdown notes and frontmatter. Relations are stored as Obsidian wikilinks, and view settings are saved in the database file.

This separation is explicit:

| Element | Note Database storage |
|---|---|
| Database definition | Markdown file with `db_view: true` |
| Records | Existing Markdown notes |
| Properties | Frontmatter in those notes |
| Relations | Obsidian wikilinks |
| Templates | Obsidian Templates or Templater files |
| Views | Saved configuration in the database file |

Because the rows remain source notes, edits made in the full database view write back to those files. A status change in Board view is therefore available to Table, List, Calendar, and other views. The plugin also supports source rules based on folders, tags, properties, links, and expressions.

#### View and editing model

Note Database’s view set covers the four requested categories directly:

- **Table** is optimized for dense editing, keyboard navigation, range selection, copy/paste, fill, and bulk changes.
- **Board** supports grouped columns, subgroups, card fields, covers, colored options, batch selection, and custom group ordering.
- **Calendar** supports month, week, and day views based on date or datetime properties.
- **List** provides a compact index for directories, tasks, and lightweight records.

Its Calendar and Timeline support drag and resize behavior for dates and date ranges. The 1.2.0 release added month, week, and day Calendar scales and day, week, month, and quarter Timeline scales. ([Note Database release 1.2.0](https://github.com/pangy9/obsidian-note-database/releases))

The plugin documents per-view filters, sorting, grouping, visible properties, title fields, and layouts. It also supports manual order, facet chips, result limits, and source-aware record creation.

#### Filtering, formulas, relations, and rollups

Note Database can combine source rules and filters with AND, OR, and NOT. It supports filtering by folder, tag, property, link, or expression. Sorting and grouping can be configured independently for each view, and Board view can use subgroups.

Formula support is extensive for a local plugin. The formula editor provides field references, syntax highlighting, live previews, helper functions, and step-by-step substitutions. Documented helpers include date calculations, rounding, conditional logic, concatenation, minimum and maximum values, and date offsets. Formula results can optionally be synchronized back to frontmatter, although computed fields can also remain virtual.

Relations use native Obsidian wikilinks. Rollups can calculate count, sum, average, or list values from linked notes. Recent release notes describe improvements to relation indicators, rollup references, property renames, failed-write rollback, and concurrent-conflict reporting. ([Note Database release notes](https://github.com/pangy9/obsidian-note-database/releases))

The plugin also provides typed bulk editing, transaction previews, rollback attempts, single-step undo, keyboard workflows, templates for new records, conditional formatting, group summaries, covers, icons, and chart drilldowns.

#### Embeds and dependencies

Embedded Note Database views are useful but have an important limitation: embedded records are read-only. The embed still retains view switching, filters, sorting, grouping, computed values, and copy/export tools, but a user must open the full database view to edit records directly.

Native previews for supported record and internal-note links require Obsidian’s core Page Preview plugin to be enabled. That is a small dependency, but it matters when comparing “standalone” behavior.

The plugin supports CSV plus Markdown ZIP export and import. It can also convert Obsidian `.base` files, attempting to preserve source rules, column order, column widths, sorting, grouping, and Cards/List information. The wording is “tries to preserve,” not a guarantee of exact conversion.

#### Strengths

Note Database is strongest for users who want a database editor that remains visibly and structurally part of the Obsidian vault.

Its strengths include:

- All four requested views plus Gallery, Chart, and Timeline.
- Explicitly shared Markdown note records.
- Direct editing of frontmatter and file names.
- Strong spreadsheet-like Table workflows.
- Relations and rollups stored as ordinary wikilinks.
- Formula previews and optional formula-result synchronization.
- AND/OR/NOT source logic.
- Bulk editing with transaction previews and rollback attempts.
- Templates through Obsidian Templates or Templater.
- CSV plus Markdown ZIP round trips.
- `.base` conversion for users coming from core Bases.
- Mobile-specific fixes for iPad and phone interfaces.
- Local operation with no external transmission of vault content.
- MIT licensing.

The recent release material also suggests active maintenance: fixes address stale properties, note renames, grouped-record refresh, relation states, formula saving, mobile layout, and concurrent conflicts. ([Note Database 1.2.9 release](https://github.com/pangy9/obsidian-note-database/releases))

#### Weaknesses and parity gaps

The most important limitation is that full editing and embedded editing are different experiences. Notion’s linked database views remain interactive in place, whereas Note Database’s embedded records are read-only.

The plugin also introduces a database configuration file or configuration object in addition to the source notes. This is still transparent Markdown, but it is more structured than simply pointing a core view at a folder. Users must back up and synchronize both the records and the database configuration.

Relations are based on wikilinks, which is a strong local model but not identical to Notion’s database relation identifiers. Renames and out-of-scope links have received several fixes, but the release notes themselves show that relation and rename handling is an active reliability area.

The available materials do not provide a comparable large-vault performance result, a formal collaboration model, or a guarantee that every Notion formula, rollup, view setting, and linked data source will convert. It is a strong local database engine, not a drop-in Notion workspace.

### Notion Bases versus Note Database

Both plugins cover the requested views, so the decision is best made on shared axes rather than on labels.

| Axis | Notion Bases | Note Database | Practical judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| View breadth | Seven views, including the requested four, Chart, Gallery, and Timeline | Seven views, including the requested four, Chart, Gallery, and Timeline | Essentially tied |
| Primary source model | Folder of Markdown rows; frontmatter stores values; `_database.md` stores schema/views | Source rules select Markdown notes; database configuration is stored in a Markdown database file | Notion Bases feels more folder-database oriented; Note Database is more source-rule oriented |
| Table workflow | Strong inline editing, pinned columns, aggregation footer, bulk row actions | Strong spreadsheet workflow, range selection, fill, copy/paste, typed bulk editing, undo | Note Database is particularly strong for heavy editing |
| Relations and rollups | Relations, lookups, seven documented rollup functions, self-relation subtasks | Wikilink relations, count/sum/average/list rollups, formula references | Notion Bases advertises broader relation terminology; Note Database emphasizes local wikilinks and safe editing |
| Import/export | CSV import/export | CSV plus Markdown ZIP and `.base` conversion | Note Database has the more explicit Obsidian migration path |
| Embeds | Multi-view embeds, including pinned view types | View switching and calculations remain available, but embedded records are read-only | Notion Bases has the stronger embedded-editing claim |
| Dependencies | Obsidian 1.8.7 or later; desktop and mobile documented | Core Page Preview needed for native previews; mobile fixes documented | Neither is entirely free of operational caveats |
| Maintenance signal | Community listing and continuing 1.13.0 release material | Community listing and continuing 1.2.x release material | Both appear active in the supplied snapshot |
| License and ownership | GPL v3 | MIT | Relevant mainly for redistribution and customization |
| Best fit | Users wanting the broadest Notion-like surface | Users wanting a deeply Markdown-native Obsidian database editor | Choose according to workflow, not view coverage |

The evidence does not establish one uncontested winner. **Notion Bases is the feature-breadth leader**, particularly for view variety, column types, embedded views, and Notion-like terminology. **Note Database is the stronger Obsidian-native alternative** when spreadsheet editing, `.base` conversion, Markdown ZIP export, transaction handling, and explicit wikilink-backed relations matter more.

## 4. Core Bases and modular combinations

### Core Obsidian Bases: a stable foundation, not a complete replacement

Obsidian’s core Bases plugin is important because it changes the default answer for many database-like tasks. It is built into Obsidian rather than installed as a community plugin, reads note properties, stores view definitions in `.base` files, and edits note properties directly.

The current descriptions supplied for the 2026 ecosystem list four core layouts: Table, List, Cards, and Map. Cards and Map are useful, but they are not the requested Board/Kanban and Calendar views. ([Core Bases view description](https://vaultpicks.net/obsidian-bases-tutorial/); [Obsidian Bases overview](https://obsidian.md/help/bases))

Core Bases therefore covers:

- Table: yes.
- List: yes.
- Board/Kanban: not documented in the core set.
- Calendar: not documented in the core set.

The third-party Notion Bases comparison reaches the same practical conclusion, although its documentation contains a small version discrepancy: one table counts six Core Bases column types and the project site counts seven. Both agree that Core Bases lacks the requested Board and Calendar views. ([Notion Bases comparison](https://bgarciamoura.github.io/obsidian-notion-bases-plugin/))

#### Core strengths

Core Bases is the safest starting point for users who want:

- No installation or community-plugin dependency.
- A visual Table/List/Card/Map view over existing notes.
- Inline property editing.
- Local Markdown storage.
- A `.base` configuration file.
- Mobile availability as part of Obsidian.
- Obsidian-team maintenance that moves with the application.
- Simple filters, sorting, grouping, formulas, and summaries.

It is especially good for reading lists, meeting indexes, project inventories, contact notes, and other note-level records whose properties are already consistent.

Core Bases also has a useful stability advantage over a collection of abandoned database plugins. It is part of the application, although that does not mean its syntax is static. A community guide reports that Bases arrived in Obsidian 1.9, became generally available in 1.9.10, and underwent breaking formula and `.base`-format changes in 1.9.2. Users following older tutorials may therefore encounter invalid formulas or incompatible base files. ([Bases version history](https://vaultpicks.net/obsidian-bases-tutorial/))

#### Core limitations

Core Bases is not a task database. It reads note-level properties rather than the individual Markdown checkboxes inside notes. A feature-request discussion explains that the cache knows a task exists and where it is located but does not expose the task’s text and details to Bases. Users who want task-level Bases records commonly promote each task to its own note or maintain a note-level property such as an open-task count. ([Bases task discussion](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/bases-support-for-tasks/103074))

Core Bases is also not documented as having native Notion-style relations and rollups in the supplied comparison material. Its formulas can be flexible for combining properties, but they do not by themselves provide a cross-database relation model.

Finally, a core Base can begin with a broad vault scope. That is powerful, but it requires careful global filters and a deliberate new-note destination. The forum comparison notes that Obsidian’s flexible all-vault model can make it harder to enforce the bounded, internally consistent property options of a Notion database. ([Obsidian Bases versus Notion](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/q-a-are-obsidian-bases-the-same-as-notion-database/112363))

### Power Bases plus Core Bases: the strongest modular four-view route

Power Bases is an add-on to core Bases. It documents six additional views or enhanced view types: Kanban, Calendar, Gantt-style Timeline, Chart, Gallery, and a richer Table. Core Bases supplies Table, Cards, and List, so the combination covers all four requested categories. ([Power Bases project](https://github.com/obsidian-power-plugins/obsidian-power-bases))

This is a genuine shared-source combination. Power Bases continues to use ordinary Obsidian notes and ordinary frontmatter. A Board card represents a note, moving it between lanes writes the selected property to that note, and Calendar movement writes dates back to the note. The core and Power views operate on the same Base data rather than importing the records into a separate database.

#### What Power Bases adds

For Board/Kanban workflows, Power Bases documents:

- Dragging cards between lanes to change a property.
- Manual row order.
- Swimlanes.
- WIP limits.
- Lane rules.
- Lane totals.
- Bulk card movement.
- Touch interaction.

For Calendar workflows, it documents:

- Month and week modes.
- Drag-to-reschedule.
- Double-click-to-create.
- Date properties as the source of event placement.

For Table workflows, it adds:

- Ten extra field types.
- A column menu.
- A formula editor with live preview.
- Number and date formatting.
- Bars, rings, and stars.
- Rollups and subtotals.
- Value colors.
- CSV import.
- Batch undo.

It also documents Gantt dependencies, milestones, progress fills, chart views, and image galleries.

#### Strengths

Power Bases is the best modular option when a user wants to keep core Bases as the underlying note/property engine while adding Board and Calendar behavior. Its advantages are:

- One shared Markdown/frontmatter data model.
- Core Table and List retained alongside Power views.
- Board and Calendar write back to the same notes.
- Stronger drag-and-drop semantics than core Cards.
- CSV import and starter templates.
- Formula editing and relation-style rollups.
- Mobile support claimed by the project.
- No proprietary row database.
- Large-vault rendering designed around incremental loading.

The project says it is used daily at 20,000 notes and has no row limit. That is an operational claim from the project, not an independently verified large-vault result, so it should be treated as an encouraging signal rather than a guaranteed capacity figure. ([Power Bases scale claim](https://github.com/obsidian-power-plugins/obsidian-power-bases))

#### Weaknesses and caveats

Power Bases requires Obsidian 1.10.2 or newer with core Bases enabled. It is therefore not a standalone replacement and inherits core Bases’ file-scope and property-shape assumptions.

The project is built and maintained by one person. That is not evidence of poor quality, but it is a narrower maintenance base than an Obsidian core feature or a large established plugin. The supplied documentation does not provide a standardized compatibility matrix across desktop and mobile versions or an independent performance comparison.

Power Bases also has one opt-in network feature: Place-field address autocomplete can query OpenStreetMap. Other view, formula, rollup, and CSV operations are documented as local. Users with strict offline requirements should disable that feature.

The List view comes from core Bases, not Power Bases itself. If a future core or plugin compatibility issue affects List, Power Bases does not independently replace it.

### Kanban Action Planner plus Core Bases

Kanban Action Planner is a more focused extension built on Obsidian Bases. It turns a Base over notes into a Board and Calendar workflow. The chosen status property becomes Board columns; dragging a card changes that status in the note’s frontmatter. The same notes can then be plotted on day, week, month, quarter, or year calendars, with dragged dates written back to the note. ([Kanban Action Planner description](https://www.dsebastien.net/how-i-turned-my-obsidian-notes-into-kanban-boards/))

This is attractive for users whose main requirement is “the same note collection as a Board and a Calendar.” It supports projects, tasks, articles, videos, goals, and other note types rather than only checklist items.

The plugin also documents:

- Swimlanes by note type or another property.
- Auto-sorting by properties or Base formulas.
- Typed search such as `status:active OR due:overdue`.
- Relationship visualization.
- A triage mode for incomplete or inconsistent metadata.

Its main caveat is schema discipline. If some notes use `reading` and others use `in progress`, the Board creates separate columns. The author describes state-machine automation as a future direction rather than a current documented feature.

Core Bases can provide Table, List, Cards, and Map alongside the Action Planner’s Board and Calendar, but the supplied material does not document the resulting combination as one fully integrated seven-view database engine. It is best understood as a focused Board/Calendar extension over a shared note source, not as a complete alternative to Notion Bases or Note Database.

### Dataview plus Kanban plus Calendar or Tasks

The older modular route combines:

- Dataview for metadata tables, lists, calendars, and task queries.
- The classic Kanban plugin for a drag-and-drop board.
- Full Calendar or the Calendar plugin for scheduling.
- Tasks for task filtering, recurrence, and completion handling.

This combination remains powerful, especially for users who already have a large Dataview vault, but it has a fundamental synchronization problem.

Dataview can generate a list of cards grouped by metadata, but the classic Kanban plugin expects its own Markdown list to be the persistent data model. A Kanban issue discussion explains that when Dataview generates the lists, Kanban cannot know what a drag operation should write back to the rest of the vault. Generated cards therefore become a read-only card display rather than a traditional editable Kanban board. ([Kanban and Dataview issue](https://github.com/obsidian-community/obsidian-kanban/issues/321))

The combination can work if the Board is maintained separately and Dataview is treated as a reporting layer. It does not reproduce Notion’s “drag in Board, see the changed status in Table and Calendar” behavior without custom scripts and a carefully designed source model.

### Dashboard Hub: all four surfaces, but not one database

Dashboard Hub is the clearest composite workspace solution. It combines native Obsidian Bases Table, Cards, and List views with Kanban boards, Calendars, Timelines, reading tools, and activity logs. It works on desktop and mobile with Obsidian 1.10.0 or later. ([Dashboard Hub](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/dashboard-hub-bases-kanban-calendar-reading-memos-connected-by-a-timeline/116453))

Its Kanban cards are regular vault notes grouped by a frontmatter status field. Its Calendar is backed by Timeline files, and rescheduling an event updates the scheduled-day file. Its activity history records Kanban moves, Calendar changes, and memo changes in ordinary Markdown files.

That design has two important strengths:

- It creates a coherent dashboard without requiring an external database.
- It records actions as searchable, Git-compatible Markdown history.

It also has a decisive limitation for the original question: the sources describe separate note-backed Kanban, Timeline-backed Calendar, and Bases-backed Table/List components rather than four views over one relational database schema. Dashboard Hub is therefore a strong “Notion-style workspace” but not a proven single-database replacement.

The project is explicitly still evolving and asks for feedback on mobile layout behavior and compatibility with existing Bases and Kanban workflows. It should be chosen for its dashboard and activity-log model, not for exact Notion database parity.

## 5. Near matches and specialized alternatives

### Database Views for Obsidian: a strong three-view near-match

Database Views for Obsidian, maintained in the `ekmungi/obsidian-database-plugin` project, documents Table, Kanban, Calendar, and Timeline/Gantt views over Markdown files. It does not name a List view, so it is a near-match rather than a full answer to the requested four-view set. ([Database Views release 0.15.0](https://github.com/ekmungi/obsidian-database-plugin/releases))

#### Data model

The plugin treats a folder of Markdown notes as a database. YAML frontmatter becomes the data source, a `.database.json` file defines the schema, and a `.dbview` file opens the database view. It can optionally scan recursive subfolders. Code blocks embed interactive views inside ordinary notes.

The source model is shared across its documented views. Inline edits write directly to frontmatter, and changes made in one open view refresh other views over the same database. Relations link notes in other database folders, and bidirectional relations can create and synchronize reverse columns.

#### Capabilities

The plugin documents:

- Inline editing of text, numbers, dates, select, multi-select, checkbox, and relation fields.
- Table sorting, filtering, search, column visibility, resizing, and reordering.
- Kanban drag-and-drop grouped by a select or multi-select property.
- Calendar drag-to-reschedule.
- Timeline zoom and date-range editing.
- Bidirectional relations.
- Read-only rollups.
- Templates.
- View tabs and persistent view-specific settings.
- Codeblock embedding.
- Automatic discovery of frontmatter properties.
- Bulk row deletion.

The release material also reports automatic saving of view settings and 234 passing tests in one release entry. That is useful project evidence, but it does not establish large-vault performance or a desktop/mobile compatibility guarantee. ([Database Views tags and releases](https://github.com/ekmungi/obsidian-database-plugin/tags))

#### Strengths

Database Views is attractive when the user wants a folder-based database with strong direct editing and Board/Calendar behavior. Its bidirectional relation model is more ambitious than a view-only query system, and its `.database.json` schema can enforce property types, select options, colors, and templates.

It also has no external plugin dependency according to its comparison table.

#### Weaknesses

The missing documented List view is the clearest functional gap. Timeline is not a substitute for List.

Installation is another concern. The release page emphasizes BRAT for beta testing and manual copying of `main.js`, `manifest.json`, and `styles.css`. The README mentions a Community Plugins registry submission, but the supplied material does not independently confirm ordinary stable availability through the Community Plugins browser.

Relations have a concrete file-system boundary: renaming a linked file inside Obsidian works, but renaming it externally through a file manager or cloud sync can leave stale backlinks that require manual frontmatter repair. That is a meaningful Notion parity gap for users who rename or sync vault files outside Obsidian.

### Obsidian Projects: historically close, currently unsafe as a recommendation

Projects was one of the earliest clear Notion-like view systems for Obsidian. It collected notes from folders, tags, and Dataview queries and provided Table, Board, Calendar, and Gallery views over the same notes. ([Projects documentation](https://acylation.github.io/obsidian-projects-docs/); [Projects demonstration](https://nicolevanderhoeven.com/blog/20221107-notion-database-views-in-obsidian/))

Its model was appealing:

- Existing notes were the records.
- Properties supplied structured fields.
- Multiple views represented the same set of notes.
- Templates could be configured for projects.
- Filtering, sorting, coloring, Templater, Dataview, and Full Calendar integrations were documented.

However, Projects is no longer a current first-choice option. The maintainer announced discontinuation in May 2025 because he was no longer using Obsidian or following the plugin ecosystem. A July 18, 2025 edit says the plugin was removed from the Community Plugins list and recommends BRAT for continued use. ([Projects repository](https://github.com/obsmd-projects/obsidian-projects))

Projects also never documented List as one of its initial views. Its configuration was kept separately in `data.json`, and its documentation flagged sync and archive issues as operational topics. The supplied material does not establish current mobile support, formula semantics, relation support, rollups, or reliable write-back behavior.

Projects is therefore useful as historical context: it demonstrated the demand for shared note views before core Bases and newer all-in-one plugins matured. It is not a sound recommendation for a new database system that must remain maintainable.

### Database Folder: the table-first operational hub

Database Folder creates Notion-like tables over folders or tag-defined note sets. It requires Dataview and uses Dataview’s search engine to display and edit note content directly in the table. ([Database Folder documentation](https://rafaelgb.github.io/obsidian-db-folder/))

Its data model is straightforward:

- A folder or tag structure defines the table.
- Markdown files are rows.
- Frontmatter keys are columns.
- Editing the table writes to the source files.
- Editing a source file refreshes the table.

The 2026 review of Database Folder describes text, number, checkbox, date, multi-select, select validation, hidden columns, sorting, filtering, visual YAML editing, and bidirectional updates. ([Database Folder review](https://notes-automate.com/posts/review-of-obsidian-db-folder-for-database-views/))

#### View coverage and database features

Database Folder has clear Table support. Its changelog documents a Calendar view, including a fix for a Calendar z-index problem. Its List entry refers to a new List editing API, but the supplied documentation does not prove that this is a separate List layout. Kanban or Board support is not documented.

Its data capabilities are stronger than a simple table:

- Date-range, checkbox, link, number-range, text, select, tag, and task filters.
- AND/OR filter groups.
- Formula columns.
- Relations and rollups between models.
- Bidirectional relations in the later changelog.
- Bulk delete and duplicate.
- CSV import and export.
- Templates for new rows.
- Dataview query and DataviewJS sources.
- Mobile pagination and a repaired mobile Calendar view.

This makes it a good operational table hub for active projects, editorial pipelines, or CRM-like note folders. It is not an all-four Notion replacement.

#### Performance and mobile caveats

One 2026 review reports noticeable degradation above 500 files and a 3–8 second opening delay for a root view containing 3,000 dense Markdown files, depending on hardware. The review recommends dedicated directories with fewer than 500 files. These figures are one review’s observations, not a universal threshold. ([Database Folder performance review](https://notes-automate.com/posts/review-of-obsidian-db-folder-for-database-views/))

The plugin is reported to work on mobile, but wide tables can be difficult on smartphones. The changelog’s mobile support originated in an earlier release, so current compatibility should be tested against the user’s Obsidian version and vault.

Database Folder is best paired with Dataview: use Database Folder for editable operational tables and Dataview for read-only vault-wide dashboards. That combination is practical, but it does not create a shared Board view over the same data.

### Rowbase: a self-contained database with a different storage model

Rowbase provides Table, Kanban, List, Gallery, Chart, Stats, Timeline, and Dashboard views. It does not document a standalone Calendar view; the Dashboard includes an activity calendar heatmap, which is not the same thing as date-positioned database records. ([Rowbase plugin page](https://community.obsidian.md/plugins/rowbase))

Its defining difference is storage. Each database is one `.rbase` file: a human-readable CSV file with JSON column metadata. The rows therefore live in the `.rbase` file rather than as individual Markdown note records with frontmatter.

That design has real advantages:

- A complete standalone spreadsheet-like database.
- Inline editing.
- Multi-column sorting.
- Typed filters.
- Grouping.
- Formulas with cell references.
- Cross-relation aggregation.
- Relations and rollups.
- A 100-step undo/redo history.
- CSV import and CSV/JSON export.
- Mobile-responsive layouts.
- No account, telemetry, or runtime network service.

Title cells can open or create Obsidian notes, and relations can link rows across databases. The plugin is therefore compatible with an Obsidian vault, but its primary database rows are not the same as a folder of Markdown notes.

Rowbase is a good choice when the user wants a portable local spreadsheet/database file and does not require every row to be a rich note. It is a weaker choice for users specifically seeking Notion’s “every database item is a page” model or a standalone Calendar view.

### Dataview: the best query layer, not a full multi-view database

Dataview turns Markdown frontmatter and inline fields into a queryable index. Its four query types are Table, List, Task, and Calendar. Table, List, and Calendar operate at page level; Task queries operate on individual tasks. ([Dataview query types](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/queries/query-types/))

This gives Dataview direct coverage of:

- Table.
- List.
- Calendar.
- Task lists.

It does not provide a documented Board/Kanban query type.

#### Query capabilities

Dataview’s DQL supports:

- Folder, tag, and link sources.
- Metadata filters.
- Sorting.
- Grouping.
- Limiting.
- Field transformations.
- Calculated columns.
- JavaScript queries.
- Inline expressions.
- Task-level filtering.

A typical Dataview Table can filter a folder, select properties, sort by a field, and limit the result. A Calendar query places each matching page as a dot on a date. A Task query can aggregate incomplete checkboxes from across the vault and allow them to be marked complete in place. ([Dataview structure documentation](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/queries/structure/))

Dataview’s task model is unusually useful because it reaches inside note bodies. Core Bases and most note-level database plugins do not treat embedded Markdown checkboxes as individual database rows.

#### Weaknesses

Ordinary Dataview output is read-only. A Table or List result must be changed in the source note. Task queries are the exception: checking a task updates the original file. ([Dataview query documentation](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/queries/query-types/))

Dataview’s calculated metadata also has a subtle limitation. An inline DQL expression can display a calculated value, but the stored field remains the expression itself. That means later filtering may compare against the expression string rather than the displayed result. ([Dataview FAQ](https://blacksmithgu.github.io/obsidian-dataview/resources/faq/))

DataviewJS is powerful but requires trust because JavaScript queries run with plugin-level access and can potentially rewrite, create, or delete files or make network calls. Regular DQL is more restricted. ([Dataview plugin page](https://community.obsidian.md/plugins/dataview))

Performance depends strongly on query scope. Dataview warns that broad, memory-intensive queries can take a long time or freeze Obsidian in extreme cases, and recommends using a restrictive `FROM` clause. A 2026 comparison describes the plugin as still functional but slow-moving: version 0.5.70 was released in April 2025, and the repository had around 660 open issues at the time of that comparison. ([Bases versus Dataview comparison](https://vaultpicks.net/obsidian-bases-vs-dataview/))

A historical iOS issue reported a desktop Table query returning no results on an iPhone. That does not prove current mobile failure, but it demonstrates why mobile compatibility should be tested rather than assumed. ([Dataview mobile issue](https://github.com/blacksmithgu/obsidian-dataview/issues/1259))

Dataview is excellent for read-only dashboards, cross-note task aggregation, analytics, and code-driven views. It is not the closest single-plugin replacement for a shared, editable Notion database.

### Classic Kanban: excellent lightweight boards, not databases

The classic Kanban plugin represents lists and cards as Markdown list items. Each card is a line in a Markdown file and can be dragged between lists. ([Kanban comparison](https://medium.com/@geetduggal/tech-habits-lists-in-obsidian-kanban-vs-obsidian-bases-f613b1673d56))

Its advantages are simplicity and transparency:

- Cards are easy to inspect in source mode.
- Board movement changes the Markdown list.
- No separate relational database is required.
- It works well for lightweight lists and a few hundred tasks.

Its limitations are fundamental:

- Cards are not automatically one note per database record.
- There is no native Table, Calendar, or List view over the same cards.
- Card metadata is less structured than frontmatter properties.
- A long-standing feature request asked for rich notes or descriptions attached to cards; the issue discussion reported that nested lists were removed and that detailed information generally required creating a separate note. ([Kanban card-notes issue](https://github.com/mgmeyers/obsidian-kanban/issues/239))
- Dataview-generated lists cannot retain normal drag-and-drop write-back.

Use classic Kanban when the underlying object really is a lightweight ordered list. Use a note-backed database plugin when each card is a project, contact, article, or rich task record.

### Full Calendar Remastered plus Tasks: the best task-scheduling combination

Full Calendar Remastered is a calendar component, not a database-view replacement. It supports events from note frontmatter, daily-note event lists, journals, ICS files, CalDAV, Google Calendar, Google Tasks, and Tasks-plugin syntax. ([Full Calendar Remastered](https://github.com/obsidian-full-calendar-remastered/plugin-full-calendar))

Its Tasks integration is particularly strong:

1. Tasks are written in Markdown using Tasks syntax.
2. Undated tasks appear in a backlog.
3. A task can be dragged to a calendar time slot.
4. The plugin writes the date and time block back to the Markdown task.
5. Completion state synchronizes to the source note.

The integration supports scheduled dates, start dates, due dates, fuzzy search, path and folder filters, tags, priorities, regular expressions, and global Tasks queries. It also distinguishes scheduled and due dates: if the Calendar is configured to display due dates, a task with only a scheduled date remains in the backlog. ([Full Calendar Tasks integration](https://obsidian-full-calendar-remastered.github.io/plugin-full-calendar/user/calendars/tasks-plugin-integration/))

This is an excellent choice for task scheduling, especially when paired with Tasks. It does not supply Table, Board, or List database views over the same task records.

Operationally, the project reports a 7.2 MB bundled `main.js` with a 380 ms load time for the Community Plugins artifact, while a self-built production bundle can be smaller. The project also discloses reliance on a monthly community subsidy for AI development tools. Those disclosures do not establish poor reliability, but they are relevant maintenance and startup considerations. ([Full Calendar project README](https://github.com/obsidian-full-calendar-remastered/plugin-full-calendar))

The Tasks plugin itself supports due dates, recurring tasks, done dates, filtering, grouping, sorting, and source-file updates. Its README warns that displaying many hundreds or thousands of tasks can make Obsidian’s editing performance very slow. ([Tasks plugin](https://github.com/obsidian-tasks-group/obsidian-tasks))

### DataLoom: insufficient evidence for the requested views

DataLoom is described as a Notion- and spreadsheet-inspired database plugin for desktop and mobile. The current Community Plugins description says it is a fork of the original `decaf-dev/obsidian-dataloom` project and that the original is no longer maintained, while the fork continues development. ([DataLoom listing](https://community.obsidian.md/plugins/obisidian-dataloom))

However, the supplied description names general concepts such as view types, sources, imports, exports, undo/redo, and mobile support without naming Table, Board/Kanban, Calendar, or List views. The original maintainer explicitly stopped maintaining DataLoom after Obsidian’s native table editor arrived, citing the project’s complexity and missing integrations. ([DataLoom maintenance notice](https://github.com/decaf-dev/obsidian-dataloom/issues/958))

The fork documents one GitHub API request for its release-notes modal and no telemetry or other network requests. That is useful privacy information, but it does not establish the requested multi-view coverage. DataLoom should therefore be treated as an unverified database-oriented option, not a recommendation for Notion parity.

### Notion Database Sync: an integration bridge, not a replacement

The Notion Database Sync plugin is easy to confuse with a local database replacement because of its name. It synchronizes the active Markdown note with a selected remote Notion database. It can push the current note to Notion, pull a linked Notion page into the note, and map frontmatter properties. It does not provide a local Table, Board, Calendar, and List database engine. ([Notion Database Sync](https://github.com/wj0s3ph/obsidian-notion-plugin))

It also does not write several Notion property types, including formulas and rollups. Setup requires a Notion integration token, shared database access, and remote permissions. Use it when a workflow must bridge Obsidian and Notion, not when the objective is to replace Notion’s database views inside Obsidian.

## 6. Comparison by practical database capability

### Filtering, sorting, grouping, and manual order

Notion provides view-specific filters, sorts, groups, sub-groups, nested AND/OR filters, manual group ordering, and search over titles and properties. Its Board view can group by status, person, select, multi-select, or other supported property types. ([Notion view documentation](https://www.notion.com/help/views-filters-and-sorts); [Notion Board documentation](https://www.notion.com/help/boards))

The leading Obsidian candidates compare as follows:

| Capability | Notion Bases | Note Database | Power Bases + Core | Database Views |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Filters | Type-aware operators and AND/OR groups | Source rules plus AND/OR/NOT, chips, expressions | Core filters plus enhanced view controls | Column filters and full-text search |
| Sorting | Multi-column priority ordering | Multi-column, manual order, view-specific state | Multi-column, manual card order, summaries | Header and multi-level sorting |
| Grouping | Groups and sub-groups | Groups, subgroups, custom group order | Swimlanes, lane rules, WIP limits | Board grouping and optional timeline grouping |
| Board movement | Writes a select/status value | Writes the underlying property | Writes the underlying property | Writes frontmatter |
| Manual order | Documented table and board ordering | Explicit manual order | Manual order is treated as real data | View-specific order; less relational context |
| Search | Database title/property search | Search and facet chips | Type-to-filter boxes | Full-text search across fields |

Notion Bases is strong for users who want a visual interface with minimal code. Note Database is stronger when filters need source rules, logical negation, manual order, and detailed editing controls. Power Bases adds the most Kanban-specific behavior, particularly WIP limits, swimlanes, lane totals, and lane rules.

Dataview remains more expressive for users willing to write DQL. It can fetch from folders, tags, links, and complex combinations, then filter, sort, group, flatten, and limit results. Its trade-off is that the query itself becomes part of the workflow and the result is normally read-only.

Database Folder is practical for column-based operations but depends on Dataview and folder or tag scope. Rowbase offers strong typed filtering and grouping, but its rows belong to the `.rbase` file rather than the Markdown note graph.

Manual order deserves special attention. Notion can preserve user-defined Board and group order. An older 2025 comparison reported that Dataview and core Bases lacked a Notion-like custom ordering mechanism at that time, although that observation was qualified and should not be treated as a definitive statement about every current version. ([2025 Bases/Kanban comparison](https://medium.com/@geetduggal/tech-habits-lists-in-obsidian-kanban-vs-obsidian-bases-f613b1673d56))

### Properties and schema discipline

Notion scopes select and multi-select options to the database. Obsidian’s properties are generally vault-level note metadata, so different databases may encounter the same property name with inconsistent values or types.

The major candidates handle this differently:

- **Notion Bases** infers and manages 18 column types within its database folder.
- **Note Database** lets users define display names, frontmatter keys, types, option colors, status presets, and source rules.
- **Power Bases** adds field types and visual formatting on top of ordinary frontmatter.
- **Database Views** stores a typed `.database.json` schema and can filter records with a `dbViewType` property.
- **Database Folder** discovers frontmatter and lets users configure select, tag, date, formula, relation, and rollup columns.
- **Dataview** is the most permissive: it can read YAML frontmatter and inline fields, but that flexibility increases inconsistency risk.
- **Rowbase** defines its own typed schema inside the `.rbase` file.

The practical consequence is that rich database views require a stable record schema. A consistent `type`, `status`, `date`, and relation convention matters more than the plugin brand. Core Bases documentation emphasizes that every note is a possible row and every property is a possible column, so users should explicitly filter to the intended record type.

### Formulas, relations, rollups, and calculated values

The plugins are not equivalent even when each advertises formulas or rollups.

| Capability | Strongest options | Main qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Spreadsheet formulas | Notion Bases, Note Database, Power Bases | Syntax and function semantics are not guaranteed to match Notion |
| Core property formulas | Core Bases | Good for note-level calculations, but not a full relation engine |
| Relations | Notion Bases, Note Database, Database Views, Database Folder, Rowbase | File links and relation identifiers behave differently |
| Rollups | Notion Bases, Note Database, Power Bases, Database Folder, Rowbase | Function sets and cross-database behavior vary |
| Task-level calculations | Dataview, Tasks | Note-level Bases plugins do not natively read embedded checkbox details |
| Formula persistence | Note Database, Database Folder, selected Core/Power workflows | Virtual and stored formula values have different synchronization consequences |

Notion Bases provides the broadest advertised relation vocabulary: Relation, Lookup, and Rollup columns, with seven rollup functions. It also supports self-relations for subtasks.

Note Database’s relation model is more explicitly Obsidian-native. Links are ordinary wikilinks in frontmatter, and rollups calculate count, sum, average, or list values from linked notes. Release notes mention updating dependent formulas and rollups when properties are renamed, which is an important local-file reliability feature.

Power Bases supports rollups that follow link properties and can aggregate values from linked notes in both directions. It also provides formula editing and display-only number formatting.

Database Views has bidirectional relations and computed read-only rollups. Its external-rename limitation is significant: a relation stored as a file link can become stale if the file is renamed outside Obsidian or by a cloud-sync process that presents a delete-and-create sequence.

Database Folder has a long changelog history for formulas, relations, rollups, bidirectional relations, task-count rollups, and formulas inside rollups. The evidence confirms capability but does not establish exact semantic equivalence with Notion.

Rowbase supports cell formulas, cross-relation aggregation, and rollups inside its own file model. It is a stronger spreadsheet database than a Markdown-note database.

Dataview can calculate values dynamically, but a calculated inline field may remain an expression in the stored metadata. That means displayed value, stored value, and filterable value can diverge.

### Inline editing, bulk changes, and write-back

Notion’s strength is that the database itself is the editing surface. The best Obsidian matches approach that behavior:

- **Notion Bases**: inline Table editing, Board card movement, Calendar date changes, bulk delete/duplicate/move.
- **Note Database**: inline typed editing, file renaming, range selection, copy/paste, fill, bulk editing, rollback attempts, and undo.
- **Power Bases**: inline typed editing, Board and Calendar write-back, batch undo, bulk card actions.
- **Database Views**: inline editing across views, direct frontmatter write-back, relation synchronization.
- **Database Folder**: direct cell editing that writes to frontmatter.
- **Rowbase**: direct editing inside the `.rbase` database.
- **Dataview**: ordinary query results read-only; only task interaction writes back.
- **Classic Kanban**: Board movement writes the Markdown list, but not a shared note-property database.

Embedded views introduce a major difference. Notion’s linked database views remain interactive database surfaces. Note Database explicitly keeps embedded records read-only, although it preserves view switching and calculations. Notion Bases documents interactive embeds with pinned view types. Core Bases supports embeds, but whether an embed gives the same depth of editing depends on the view and Obsidian version.

### Templates and automation

Notion templates reproduce a page structure, while database buttons and automations can change properties or trigger actions. Obsidian coverage is fragmented:

- **Note Database** supports new-record templates backed by Markdown Templates or Templater.
- **Database Views** has a multi-folder template picker.
- **Database Folder** supports templates for new rows.
- **Power Bases** provides starter templates and lane rules that can write properties when a card enters a lane.
- **Notion Bases** documents live placeholders and auto-arrangement, but the supplied feature list does not establish database-button-style automation.
- **Projects** documented note templates, but its maintenance status makes that feature a poor basis for a new system.
- **DataviewJS** can automate almost anything, but scripts require plugin-level trust and can alter files.
- **Kanban Action Planner** describes state-machine automation as a planned direction rather than a documented current capability.
- **Tasks** supplies recurrence and task editing, while Full Calendar supplies date/time scheduling.

If automation is central, the strongest current local route is usually a typed note database plus Templater, Tasks, or a carefully controlled script. No candidate shown here reproduces Notion’s collaboration-oriented automation layer in full.

### Desktop, mobile, installation, and maintenance

| Candidate | Platform and installation evidence | Main operational caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Notion Bases | Community Plugins; Obsidian 1.8.7 or later; desktop and mobile | Third-party plugin; no independent scale result |
| Note Database | Community Plugins; manual installation also documented; mobile fixes in releases | Embedded records read-only; Page Preview needed for native previews |
| Core Bases | Ships with Obsidian on desktop and mobile | Core layouts do not include documented Board and Calendar |
| Power Bases | Requires Obsidian 1.10.2 and core Bases | One-person maintenance; 20,000-note claim not independently verified |
| Database Views | BRAT/manual installation emphasized | Stable registry status and mobile support are not established in the supplied material |
| Projects | BRAT after removal from Community Plugins | Discontinued |
| Database Folder | Dataview dependency; mobile support documented in changelog and review | Current large-folder performance can degrade |
| Dataview | Community plugin; desktop and mobile use reported, with historical mobile issue | Slow feature development and broad-query performance risk |
| Rowbase | Community Plugins, manual install, or BRAT; mobile responsive | Separate `.rbase` storage; no scale result supplied |
| Dashboard Hub | Community Plugins; Obsidian 1.10.0 or later; desktop and mobile | Explicitly still evolving |
| Full Calendar Remastered | Community Plugins; desktop/mobile context through Obsidian | Large bundled artifact and ongoing project-maintenance dependency |

File-backed storage is a portability advantage, but it is not a guarantee of conflict-free synchronization. Database Views explicitly documents stale relation backlinks after external file renames. Note Database’s recent releases address rename and concurrent-write handling, but any multi-device workflow should still test conflicts with the user’s chosen sync system.

### Performance and scale

There is no comparable, independently measured performance series across these plugins, so scale claims must be treated cautiously.

The most concrete operational signals are:

- **Database Folder**: one 2026 review reports 3–8 seconds to open a view over 3,000 dense Markdown files and recommends dedicated scopes below 500 files.
- **Power Bases**: the project says it is used daily at 20,000 notes and has no row limit, but no independent result is supplied.
- **Dataview**: documentation warns that broad queries can take a long time or freeze Obsidian; restrict sources with `FROM`.
- **Tasks**: its README warns that displaying many hundreds or thousands of tasks can significantly slow Obsidian editing.
- **Full Calendar Remastered**: the Community Plugins artifact is reported as 7.2 MB with a 380 ms load time because dependencies must be bundled.
- **Rowbase**: mobile and offline operation are documented, but no vault-size threshold is supplied.
- **Notion Bases and Note Database**: both document local operation and extensive features, but the supplied material does not provide a comparable scale measurement.

Performance is affected by more than row count. Relation and rollup resolution, frontmatter parsing, full-text search, images, Calendar event density, grouping, formulas, and mobile rendering can all change the experience. Narrow source folders and consistent metadata are safer than one broad vault-wide database.

## 7. Notion migration and import limitations

### API import is not view-preserving

The official Obsidian Importer’s Notion API implementation creates an Obsidian `.base` configuration with a default Table view. The generated Base filters imported notes through a frontmatter link to the database’s `.base` file, so the imported records and the Base still share a note-backed source. ([Importer database helper](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-importer/blob/d4e05b71/src/formats/notion-api/database-helpers.ts))

That does not mean every Notion view survives. Migration guidance based on the importer documents states that:

- Only the primary view of each Notion database is imported.
- Linked data sources are not imported.
- Unsupported formulas require manual review.
- Some functions such as `name()`, `email()`, `style()`, and `unstyle()` are not converted.
- The resulting `.base` should be treated as a starting view rather than proof that all views and settings were preserved. ([Notion-to-Obsidian migration guide](https://www.obsibrain.com/blog/notion-to-obsidian-migration-a-complete-guide-and-checklist))

The importer implementation also shows that unsupported formulas can fall back to ordinary text properties. Relation and rollup conversions are approximations: one documented approach stores relations as a list of YAML links and converts a rollup count into a formula measuring the relation list length. That is useful, but it is not the same as preserving Notion’s native relation and rollup objects. ([Importer relation and formula implementation](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-importer/blob/d4e05b71/src/formats/notion-api/database-helpers.ts))

The importer’s API path queries pages in batches of 100 and depends on the Notion API version, access scope, permissions, and rate limits. A staged relation import can resolve links after referenced pages arrive in a later batch, but migration correctness still depends on the source structure and import path.

### HTML and ZIP import is page-first

A Notion HTML/ZIP export is useful when users want a token-free or offline migration of pages, attachments, hierarchy, and links. It does not preserve Notion databases as live Obsidian multi-view databases. Database views and structure must be rebuilt. ([Notion migration options](https://www.obsibrain.com/blog/notion-to-obsidian-migration-a-complete-guide-and-checklist))

This distinction is critical:

- **API import** is the better starting point when properties, formulas, relations, and database entries matter.
- **HTML/ZIP import** is better for pages and attachments when users accept rebuilding databases.
- Neither path should be assumed to preserve every Table, Board, Calendar, List, linked view, filter, sort, group, automation, or permission setting.

A forum migration report also describes rows appearing both as individual notes and as copied table content, allowing the two representations to diverge after editing. That is an anecdotal report rather than a universal importer behavior, but it reinforces the need to inspect a test migration before changing the original Notion workspace. ([Imported database report](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/handling-imported-notion-database-views-that-include-calculated-properties/66387))

### Plugin-specific migration

The candidates differ in how well they support local migration after import:

- **Note Database** has the clearest Obsidian-focused migration path: CSV plus Markdown ZIP round trips and `.base` conversion that tries to preserve source rules, column order, widths, sorting, grouping, and Cards/List information.
- **Notion Bases** supports CSV import/export but does not document full Notion view import.
- **Power Bases** supports CSV import and templates through core Bases.
- **Database Folder** supports CSV import and writes directly to frontmatter.
- **Rowbase** imports CSV and exports CSV/JSON, but its rows live in `.rbase` rather than automatically becoming rich Markdown records.
- **Dataview** requires the user to preserve or normalize frontmatter and rewrite queries.
- **Database Views** has no supplied evidence of a Notion migration workflow.
- **Projects** and **DataLoom** should not be selected for a new migration-dependent system because of maintenance uncertainty.

A migration is therefore best understood as two separate tasks:

1. Move pages and properties into local Markdown.
2. Rebuild and validate the active database views in the chosen Obsidian system.

### Collaboration and permissions remain a decisive gap

Notion supports shared databases, permission levels, comments, page collaboration, database locking, and controlled editing of data versus structure. The supplied migration guidance explicitly warns that Obsidian is not a drop-in replacement for shared Notion workspaces requiring real-time collaboration and permissions. ([Migration collaboration caveat](https://www.obsibrain.com/blog/notion-to-obsidian-migration-a-complete-guide-and-checklist))

The Obsidian plugins in this comparison are primarily local-vault tools. Some can record changes in Markdown, and Obsidian Sync or Git can distribute those files, but that is not equivalent to Notion’s simultaneous collaborative database interface. Teams should keep workflows requiring permissions, comments, and real-time shared editing in Notion or another team-oriented system.

## 8. Recommendations by goal

### Closest single-plugin option

Choose **Notion Bases** if the main goal is the broadest visual and functional approximation of Notion databases:

- All four requested views are explicit.
- The interface is intentionally Notion-like.
- Relations, lookups, rollups, formulas, subtasks, charts, timelines, CSV, and bulk actions are documented.
- Table, Board, Calendar, and List use the same Markdown records.
- Desktop and mobile support are documented.

Choose **Note Database** instead if the main goal is an Obsidian-native editing and migration workflow:

- It also covers all four requested views.
- Its source model is explicitly Markdown notes and wikilinks.
- Its Table editor is especially strong for bulk editing and spreadsheet operations.
- Its release history emphasizes rename safety, rollback, relation handling, formula saving, mobile fixes, `.base` conversion, and CSV/Markdown ZIP export.
- Its embedded records are read-only, so it is less suitable if many dashboards must be edited directly in place.

The evidence supports a qualified two-winner conclusion:

- **Notion Bases wins on feature breadth and Notion-like surface parity.**
- **Note Database wins on explicit Obsidian-native database administration and migration tooling.**

### Best modular combination

Choose **Power Bases plus core Bases** when you want:

- One shared Markdown/frontmatter source.
- Core Table and List views.
- A real Board/Kanban with drag-to-property behavior.
- Month and week Calendar views with date write-back.
- Enhanced Table editing, formulas, rollups, summaries, charts, and CSV.
- A system that remains integrated with the core Bases engine.

This is the strongest documented modular route for all four requested categories. Its caveats are the dependency on Obsidian 1.10.2 or newer, one-person maintenance, and the absence of independent validation for the project’s 20,000-note scale claim.

Use **Kanban Action Planner plus core Bases** when the priority is a shared note-based Board and Calendar for projects, goals, articles, or tasks. It is more focused and less database-broad than Power Bases, but its status and scheduling interactions are clearly described.

### Best option by view

#### Best Table view

- **Core Bases** for a stable, built-in, simple property table.
- **Note Database** for the strongest spreadsheet-style editing, bulk changes, and `.base` conversion.
- **Notion Bases** for the richest typed columns, aggregation footer, bulk actions, and Notion-like interface.
- **Database Folder** for a table-first operational hub with direct YAML editing and validation.

#### Best Board/Kanban view

- **Power Bases** for WIP limits, swimlanes, lane rules, lane totals, manual order, and shared Core Bases data.
- **Notion Bases** for the broadest all-in-one database experience.
- **Note Database** for a full local database with Board subgroups, covers, colored options, and bulk operations.
- **Database Views** for a near-Notion Board with bidirectional relations if manual or BRAT installation is acceptable.
- **Classic Kanban** for lightweight ordered Markdown lists that do not need database properties.

#### Best Calendar view over database notes

- **Note Database** for month, week, and day Calendar views over the same records as Table and Board.
- **Notion Bases** for a polished monthly Calendar integrated with the other seven views.
- **Power Bases** for month/week Calendar scheduling within core Bases.
- **Kanban Action Planner** for a Board-to-Calendar workflow over the same note set.
- **Database Folder** if a table-first workflow only needs a documented Calendar companion.

#### Best Calendar for tasks and time blocking

Choose **Full Calendar Remastered plus Tasks**. Its backlog, drag-to-schedule workflow, date-marker mapping, time-block syntax, and completion write-back are more task-specific than general database plugins.

The cost is that this is not a Table/Board/List database. Use it alongside Note Database, Notion Bases, Core Bases, or Dataview if tasks must also appear in a broader note database.

#### Best List or read-only dashboard

- **Core Bases** for a simple built-in List of note records.
